newsitem.title: THAILAND: FOCUS-Thai stocks at eight-year-low but jitters ease.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Thai stocks at eight-year-low but jitters ease.

text.p: The Thai bourse suffered more losses to approach new eight-year lows on Thursday but analysts said the mood was less frantic as the baht stabilised and fears of an imminent currency devalution eased.
After nearly three weeks of declines, the battered Stock Exchange of Thailand (SET) key index shed another 2.35 percent to close at 557.87 points -- the lowest finish since May 1989.
The market had dropped as low as 544.10 before late fund buying pared losses, brokers said.

Talk of a possible baht devaluation over the past few days had battered the stock market and the currency. But the baht rallied late on Thursday following intervention and assurances by Thai authorities that it would not devalue the currency.
The Thai currency was quoted at 25.350/25.450 to the dollar in late dealings, compared with 26.330/26.430 late on Wednesday when it was hammered by speculators.
The Bank of Thailand on Thursday reassured investors it had no plans to devalue the currency.
"The central bank wishes to stress that there would be no devaluation or changes in the currency exchange mechanism which were mentioned by rumours," it said in a statement.

Finance Minister Amnuay Viravan also repeated the government's determination to guard the currency against speculative attacks. He said the government's defence of the baht has been, and will be, successful.
Analysts said the reassurances and intervention by the Bank of Thailand and other central banks helped stabilise the baht and, in turn, the stock market.

The central bank and the Monetary Authority of Singapore jointly intervened in foreign exchange markets on Wednesday, and other regional central banks were said to have done the same, although it was not confirmed.
The Bank of Japan said it would be prepared to intervene to support the baht if asked to do so.
"We had believed that the baht was not going to be devalued," said David Riedel, vice president of research for Salomon Brothers. "This latest attack has been beaten back."
But he said the latest assault on the currency was the third in six months and it could lead investors to be wary of investing too heavily in baht.
"I think investors are... wary of a resurgence. They have to watch it very carefully," he said.
Stock traders said local funds were encouraged by renewed currency stability and the pledge of support from the Bank of Japan, so they went bargain-hunting in afternoon dealings.

Many foreign investors, spooked by Wednesday's heavy speculative assault on the baht and worried about the underlying weakness of the Thai economy, unloaded blue chips throughout the day, brokers said.
The market has been battered lately not only by the currency but also by worries over the slowing economy, lacklustre first quarter earnings and troubled finance and propery sectors.
